lines.text: How a trierarch keeps your ships crewed, and when to use one.
By hand, you crew every ship yourself.
Pick a computer, make a worktree, start the session, paste the crew line.
That line carries the ship's secret.
Then the same four steps again, for each ship.
Twelve steps, three ships.
At two in the morning, one session ends.
Nobody restarts it. Its ship waits.
At eight thirty you notice, and start it again.
Three ships: thirteen steps by you, and one restart.
Same three ships. Now with a trierarch.
The plugin sits beside the fleet.
Each computer runs a trierarch: a plain process, not an AI.
A computer joins with one setup line, once.
It reports what it offers: harnesses, models, room.
You write one crew request per ship.
The plugin picks the computer that fits best.
And if none fits, it says why.
The trierarch makes the worktree, and registers the ship itself.
The session starts without ever seeing the secret.
A message arrives while the session is idle, so the trierarch hands it in.
At two in the morning, a session ends.
Back in seconds.
After five restarts in an hour, it stops and tells you.
Remove the request, and the ship is released.
Unpushed work is reported to you.
Each new ship: four steps by hand, or one request.
Restarts by you: one, or none.
One setup line per computer, then it keeps them crewed.
Use it when ships must stay crewed with no one watching,
when sessions spread over several computers,
and to have worktrees and secrets handled.
Skip it for a ship or two you crew yourself:
the aeolus plugin is enough there.
And in a chat client, or on Windows.
Sessions on one computer share your account; containers keep them apart.
Aeolus. The open network for people, apps and agents.
